title: The India Story Drops Its Teaser Tomorrow. Shreyas Talpade and Kajal Aggarwal Are Making a Film About the Food You Are Eating.
excerpt: A Zee Studios film about pesticide farming and food adulteration arrives in Hindi, Tamil, and Telugu on July 24. The subject matter could not be more personal for diaspora families who still buy from back home.
body:
Bollywood has always loved biopics and political dramas. But every once in a while, a film appears that touches something more visceral — the food on your plate.

The India Story, starring Shreyas Talpade and Kajal Aggarwal, is a socio-national drama about the consequences of chemical misuse in Indian agriculture. The film's teaser is set to launch digitally on Friday, June 5. The theatrical release is locked in for July 24, 2026, across Hindi, Tamil, and Telugu.

What the Film Is About

Also referred to as The India Story: Slow Poison in Progress, the film does not confine itself to one family's tragedy. It expands into a systemic crisis — the unchecked use of pesticides in Indian farming and the cascading health impacts on millions of people who consume the produce.

The narrative explores industrial negligence, weak regulatory enforcement, delayed policy responses, and the human cost of toxic chemicals infiltrating food chains and ecosystems. Think of it as Erin Brockovich meets the realities of Indian agricultural policy — where the gap between regulation and enforcement is not a bureaucratic footnote but a public health emergency.

Directed by Chettan DK and produced and written by Sagar B Shinde, the film is backed by Zee Studios. The technical crew includes cinematographer Nishant Bhagwat, music composer Mangesh Dhakde, editor Ashish Mhatre, lyricist Shakeel Azami, and sound designer Anmol Bhave.

The Cast

Shreyas Talpade has built a career navigating between mainstream entertainment and socially conscious cinema. From Iqbal to Welcome to Sajjanpur, he has a track record of bringing dignity to characters that exist outside Bollywood's star-studded comfort zone. His involvement in The India Story signals a film that takes its subject seriously.

Kajal Aggarwal, one of South India's biggest stars, brings pan-Indian appeal. Known for powerhouse performances across Telugu, Tamil, and Hindi cinema, her casting ensures the film reaches audiences in southern states where agricultural issues are felt most acutely. Murali Sharma, Manish Wadhwa, and Trisha Sarda round out the supporting cast.

Why This Film Matters for the Diaspora

If you are an NRI who has ever shipped mangoes from Ratnagiri, ordered spices from India, or worried about what your parents eat — this film is talking to you.

India's food safety infrastructure has been a topic of growing concern. Pesticide residue levels in Indian produce have been flagged by international agencies. The European Union has rejected multiple shipments of Indian spices and produce over the last several years due to chemical contamination. For diaspora families who regularly send provisions home or receive food items from India, the issue is not abstract — it is on their kitchen counter.

The film arrives at a moment when food safety conversations in India are finally moving from academic journals and activist circles into mainstream discourse. FSSAI enforcement has expanded, but the gap between testing capacity and the sheer volume of agricultural output remains enormous.

Producer Sagar B Shinde addressed the motivation directly: "We chose to tell this story because it reflects a reality that often goes unnoticed but impacts countless lives across the country. The misuse of chemicals, especially in pesticide farming, is not just an environmental concern — it is a human crisis."

The Market Timing

The India Story releases on July 24 — a week that typically sees lower theatrical competition before the Independence Day corridor heats up in August. The trilingual release strategy (Hindi, Tamil, Telugu) positions it as a pan-India play, and the Zee Studios backing ensures wide distribution.

The teaser tomorrow will be the first real glimpse of tone and execution. A film about food adulteration could go in several directions — investigative thriller, courtroom drama, social realism. The promotional tagline — "The poison was never in the fields alone. It was in the silence" — suggests the filmmakers are aiming for something with weight.

What to Watch For

Whether The India Story succeeds commercially depends on whether Indian audiences are ready to watch a film about what they eat. The subject is uncomfortable by design. But in a year where Bollywood has increasingly rewarded films that engage with real-world issues — from Maatrubhumi tackling military history to Governor exploring economic crisis — there is reason to believe the market appetite for substance is growing.

For NRIs who have watched India's food safety debates from afar, this may be the first time the issue arrives not in a news article or a WhatsApp forward, but on a cinema screen with two genuine stars attached to it. That alone makes the June 5 teaser worth watching.
